Some pains, sufferings and discomforts which cannot be termed as disease include ________.
back: Childbirth pains, grief from the bereavement of a loved one, fatigue after rigorous physical labor, and normal biological aging
detail: Natural physiological and emotional experiences distinct from pathological disease. • Ref: Page 92

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
Medical treatment for diseases could be in two forms namely ________ and ________.
back: Curative (therapeutic) treatment and Preventive (prophylactic) treatment
detail: Eliminating existing pathogens vs vaccinating to avert infection. • Ref: Pages 92-93

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
The use of Statistical normality in explaining disease requires the use of specie's average measurement levels as a yardstick. The indices are ________.
back: Blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose levels, heart rate, and white blood cell count
detail: Statistical deviations beyond standard standard deviations define clinical abnormality. • Ref: Pages 93-94

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q10]
________ is a situation when an individual consciously feels that they are unhealthy as a result of pain and discomfort. ________ is a form of medical problem in the human body and system. ________ is a manifestation of such medical problem.
back: Illness (subjective feeling); Disease (objective biological pathology); Sickness (social role / societal recognition)
detail: The classic sociological triad: Disease (pathology), Illness (subjective experience), Sickness (social status). • Ref: Pages 94-95

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q11]
What are public goods?
back: Commodities or services provided to all members of a society, typically by the government, that are non-excludable and non-rivalrous in consumption.
detail: Examples include public sanitation, clean air, street lighting, and herd immunity from mass vaccination. • Ref: Pages 95-96

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q12]
Public goods have two main characteristics. Name and briefly explain each: ________ and ________.
back: (i) Non-excludability: No individual can be effectively excluded from using the good once provided, even if they refuse to pay (free-rider problem). (ii) Non-rivalry: One individual's consumption does not reduce the availability or quality of the good for others.
detail: Core economic criteria distinguishing public goods from private commodities. • Ref: Pages 95-96

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q13]
What are the main distributive factors of public goods in Nigeria?
back: Political patronage, ethnic considerations, urban-rural disparity, fiscal allocations, and bureaucratic corruption
detail: Skewed distribution leads to severe healthcare marginalization in rural communities. • Ref: Pages 96-97

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q14]
What are the roles government plays in the provision of healthcare? (i), (ii), (iii), (iv).
back: (i) Direct financing and building of primary, secondary, and tertiary health infrastructure. (ii) Regulatory oversight, standard setting, and drug licensing (via NAFDAC). (iii) Disease surveillance, epidemic outbreak control, and mass immunizations. (iv) Subsidizing essential maternal and child healthcare services.
detail: Sovereign duty under the right to health. • Ref: Pages 97-98

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q15]
Some healthcare issues that require ethical governance in Nigeria are ________.
back: Equitable access to essential medicines, patient informed consent, clinical trial ethics, brain drain (emigration of doctors/nurses), and end-of-life care
detail: Bioethical challenges in developing healthcare systems. • Ref: Pages 98-99

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q16]
The four principles of ethics in healthcare provision are ________, ________, ________, and ________.
back: Autonomy, Beneficence, Non-maleficence, and Justice (Beauchamp & Childress)
detail: Foundational pillar of modern medical bioethics. • Ref: Pages 99-100

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q17]
Why did members of the Hausa-Fulani ethnic group oppose the Federal Government of Nigeria's decision to vaccinate children in a global polio eradication drive in 2003?
back: Rumors and religious-political suspicions arose that the oral polio vaccines were contaminated with anti-fertility agents and HIV virus by Western powers to depopulate Muslim communities.
detail: Led to an 11-month boycott across Kano, Kaduna, and Zamfara States until independent local testing verified safety. • Ref: Pages 100-101

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q18]
Three examples of the United Nations framework for preventing conflicts in health ethical governance are ________, ________, and ________.
back: The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), the Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights (UNESCO, 2005), and the UN Guiding Principles on Health in Fragile States
detail: Global governance mechanisms establishing standards during public health emergencies. • Ref: Pages 101-102

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q19]
What is gene therapy?
back: A medical experimental technique that modifies or alters a person's genes to treat or prevent genetic disorders and hereditary diseases.
detail: Promising clinical advances alongside contentious ethical issues surrounding germline modification and genetic enhancement. • Ref: Pages 102-103

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q20]
What is healthcare delivery conflict?
back: Disputes, disagreements, and systemic friction arising among healthcare professionals, management, government authorities, and patients regarding resource distribution, wages, working conditions, or clinical negligence.
detail: Frequently manifests in recurrent strikes by medical doctors (NARD) and health workers (JOHESU). • Ref: Pages 103-104

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q21]
What are the possible consequences of healthcare delivery conflicts?
back: Preventable patient deaths, disruption of emergency medical services, erosion of public trust in healthcare systems, and economic losses.
detail: Paralyzes public hospital operations and exacerbates medical poverty. • Ref: Pages 104-105

chapter_title: Health and Conflict
front:
[Workbook Review Q22]
In what forms can healthcare delivery conflicts manifest? Name and briefly explain each: (i), (ii).
back: (i) Inter-professional rivalry conflict: Disputes between medical doctors and other allied healthcare professionals (pharmacists, nurses, laboratory scientists) over hospital leadership and salary disparities. (ii) Industrial/Labor disputes: Strike actions between healthcare worker unions and the government over unpaid hazard allowances, dilapidated equipment, and welfare conditions.
detail: Structural friction crippling the Nigerian tertiary health sector. • Ref: Pages 105-106

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q1]
Best (2006) defined ________ as the meticulous examination of any situation utilizing specific frameworks, paradigms, and methodologies.
back: Conflict Analysis
detail: Diagnostic tool to identify root causes and structural dynamics of disputes. • Ref: Page 107

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q2]
________ et al. (2000) conceived of conflict analysis as involving the systematic examination and comprehension of the conflict's reality from multiple viewpoints.
back: Simon Fisher (Responding to Conflict)
detail: Multi-perspectival understanding preventing biased interventions. • Ref: Pages 107-108

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q3]
________ is a pragmatic instrument that assists conflict managers in efficiently devising their intervention strategies.
back: Conflict Analysis
detail: Diagnostic foundation for tailored peacebuilding. • Ref: Page 108

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q4]
The three fundamental components of peace practice are: conflict analysis; conflict tracking and ________.
back: Conflict Evaluation / Impact Assessment (or Peacebuilding Evaluation)
detail: Integrated cycle of intervention design, monitoring, and impact evaluation. • Ref: Pages 108-109

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q5]
The phrase 'Peace Practice' encompasses the full range of peacekeeping, peace-making, and peacebuilding, together referred to as the ________.
back: Peace Continuum / Peace Architecture
detail: Boutros Boutros-Ghali's Agenda for Peace taxonomy. • Ref: Page 109

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q6]
Conflict tracking employs the systematic methodology known as the ________.
back: Conflict Early Warning System (CEWS) / Monitoring Matrix
detail: Continuous observation of dynamic conflict indicators. • Ref: Pages 109-110

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q7]
The acronym EWS stands for ________.
back: Early Warning System
detail: Surveillance framework warning decision-makers of impending violent escalations. • Ref: Page 110

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
________ represents the final stage in the continuum of peace practice.
back: Peacebuilding / Post-conflict Reconstruction (Sustainable Peace)
detail: Structural reforms to prevent conflict recurrence. • Ref: Pages 110-111

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
IDASA (2004, p.8) states that 'conflict analysis comprises three stages: pre-conflict analysis, intervention analysis, and ________.'
back: Post-conflict (or Impact) analysis
detail: Three temporal assessment phases for peace practitioners. • Ref: Page 111

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q10]
The major components of conflict analysis are: Issues, Actors, Conflict Stages, and ________ analysis.
back: Context (or Structural Dynamics)
detail: The 4 essential dimensions of any comprehensive conflict audit. • Ref: Pages 111-112

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q11]
By ________ in a conflict we refer to individuals or entities who are either directly or indirectly involved in a conflict situation.
back: Actors (or Stakeholders)
detail: Entities with interests, stakes, or influence in the conflict. • Ref: Page 112

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q12]
Actors in a conflict may also be referred to as ________ or ________.
back: Stakeholders or Conflict Parties
detail: Entities whose goals are perceived as incompatible. • Ref: Pages 112-113

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q13]
Albert (2001) classified conflict stakeholders into primary, secondary, and ________ Parties.
back: Tertiary (Shadow / External)
detail: Classification based on directness of involvement. • Ref: Page 113

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q14]
The ________ parties are typically seen as those directly engaged in the conflict.
back: Primary
detail: Direct antagonists who have direct vested interests in the outcome. • Ref: Page 113

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q15]
The ________ parties are individuals or groups indirectly engaged in the conflict due to their association with the principal parties.
back: Secondary
detail: Allies, financial sponsors, or sympathizers. • Ref: Pages 113-114

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q16]
The ________ parties are also referred to as allies.
back: Secondary
detail: Parties lending political, military, or logistic backing. • Ref: Page 114

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q17]
________ analysis fundamentally involves the examination of a conflict's historical background.
back: Context (or Historical / Root Cause)
detail: Traces colonial, demographic, and structural grievances over time. • Ref: Page 114

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q18]
The ________ stage of conflict could also be called the formation or latent stage.
back: Pre-conflict (Latent / Incipient)
detail: Grievances exist beneath the surface without active violence. • Ref: Pages 114-115

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q19]
At the ________ stage of conflict, the parties might engage in some sort of quarrelling as communication begins to be strained.
back: Confrontation (Escalation)
detail: Polarization worsens and verbal attacks replace constructive engagement. • Ref: Page 115

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q20]
The height or peak of conflict situations is known as the ________ stage.
back: Crisis (Peak / Climax / Acute)
detail: Open warfare, casualties, and maximum hostility. • Ref: Pages 115-116

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q21]
The ________ stage of conflict explains conflict de-escalation.
back: De-escalation (Stalemate / Hurting Stalemate / Negotiation)
detail: Parties realize mutually hurting stalemate and seek mediation. • Ref: Page 116

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q22]
What stage of conflict is largely characterized by two levels of activities: improvement and transformation?
back: Post-conflict (Resolution / Outcome / Transformation)
detail: Rebuilding relationships and reforming underlying social structures. • Ref: Pages 116-117

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q23]
In the onion-doughnut analysis, the outer layer of the onion represents the ________ the actors express publicly.
back: Positions (what they say they want)
detail: Public posturing masking underlying motives. • Ref: Pages 117-118

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q24]
Also, the onion-doughnut analysis holds that while interests can often be negotiated, ________ are non-negotiable.
back: Basic Human Needs (identity, security, survival, dignity)
detail: John Burton's Basic Human Needs Theory. • Ref: Page 118

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q25]
The ABC Triangle of conflict analysis is also known as the ________.
back: Conflict Triangle (Johan Galtung's Model)
detail: Connects Attitude, Behaviour, and Contradiction (Context). • Ref: Pages 118-119

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q26]
The ABC Triangle of conflict analysis was created by peace researcher ________.
back: Johan Galtung (1969, 1996)
detail: Pioneer of modern peace studies. • Ref: Page 119

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q27]
The ________ method of conflict analysis is best situated in tracking intergroup conflicts.
back: Conflict Tree (Root, Trunk, Leaves) / Conflict Mapping
detail: Roots: structural causes; Trunk: manifest problem; Leaves: observable effects. • Ref: Pages 119-120

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q28]
The ________ analytical procedure creates two analogous islands extending from the ocean in a pyramidal shape.
back: Pillars of Conflict / Pyramid Model
detail: Demonstrates structural pillars upholding war or peace systems. • Ref: Pages 120-121

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q29]
A ________ is defined as 'a venue where knowledge is exchanged, and consensus is achieved regarding the nature of the situation, its current state, and its desired future.'
back: Conflict Analysis Workshop / Dialogue Forum
detail: Facilitated problem-solving session for stakeholders. • Ref: Pages 121-122

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q30]
________ aim to investigate and ascertain the principal facts pertinent to comprehending a specific conflict or dispute.
back: Fact-Finding Missions (Inquiries / Commissions)
detail: Neutral investigative teams gathering empirical evidence. • Ref: Page 122

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q31]
What are the paramount tasks in the issue analysis of a conflict?
back: Identifying the root/underlying causes, immediate triggers, systemic catalysts, and distinguishing tangible issues (land, money) from intangible issues (honor, identity).
detail: Clarifies the core contention points driving the dispute. • Ref: Pages 122-123

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q32]
Briefly explain the following sources for conflict analysis information: (i) Case study, (ii) Analysis Meetings/Workshops, (iii) Fact-finding missions.
back: (i) Case study: In-depth historical and sociological examination of past similar conflicts to derive insights. (ii) Analysis Workshops: Interactive forums where conflicting parties and experts map dynamics collaboratively. (iii) Fact-finding missions: On-the-ground investigative deployments by independent observers to gather verifiable evidence.
detail: Primary intelligence gathering tools for conflict mediators. • Ref: Pages 121-123

chapter_title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
front:
[Workbook Review Q33]
Briefly explain the following frameworks for analysis: (i) Onion-Doughnut model, (ii) ABC Triangle.
back: (i) Onion-Doughnut Model: Peels conflict like an onion through three layers: Outer Layer = Positions (what parties say publicly); Middle Layer = Interests (what they truly want); Core Layer = Needs (fundamental, non-negotiable human requirements for survival, identity, and security). (ii) ABC Triangle: Galtung's model examining: A = Attitudes (prejudices, stereotypes, perceptions); B = Behaviours (threats, verbal attacks, violent coercion); C = Contradiction/Context (the underlying structural dispute or incompatibility of goals).
detail: Foundational diagnostic frameworks taught across peace studies. • Ref: Pages 117-120

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q1]
According to ________, peace education promotes knowledge about the requirements of, the obstacles to, and the possibilities for achieving and maintaining peace.
back: Betty Reardon (1988)
detail: Pioneering feminist peace educator and scholar. • Ref: Page 125

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q2]
________ posited that peace education supports the development of skills, capacities, attitudes and values necessary to prevent violence, and to create the conditions conducive to peace, whether at an intrapersonal, interpersonal, intergroup, national or international level.
back: Ian Harris and John Synott (2002)
detail: Multi-level holistic peace pedagogy. • Ref: Pages 125-126

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q3]
________ referred to Peace education as a means of ensuring holistic peace in their respective domains.
back: UNICEF / UNESCO
detail: International mandate for peace education in school curricula. • Ref: Page 126

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q4]
________ posited that peace education is simply 'teaching about peace' in terms of what it is all about; why it does not (or does) exist; and how to achieve it.
back: Johan Galtung (1975) / James Page (2008)
detail: Core philosophical query of peace studies. • Ref: Pages 126-127

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q5]
The seven strategies through which teaching and learning about peace suppresses the culture of violence as outlined by the World Health Organization (WHO) are: (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii).
back: (i) Developing safe, stable and nurturing relationships between children and parents; (ii) Developing life skills in children and adolescents; (iii) Reducing the availability and misuse of alcohol; (iv) Reducing access to lethal means (guns and weapons); (v) Promoting gender equality to prevent violence against women; (vi) Changing cultural and social norms that support violence; (vii) Victim identification, care and support programmes.
detail: Evidence-based public health strategies to eliminate interpersonal violence. • Ref: Pages 127-128

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q6]
________ is the peace education directed toward the elimination of violence in all its various forms and manifestations.
back: Negative Peace Education (Education for Disarmament and Non-violence)
detail: Focuses on stopping direct physical warfare and violent crime. • Ref: Pages 128-129

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q7]
________ is the nurturing and establishment of the conditions necessary for peace to flourish.
back: Positive Peace Education (Education for Social Justice, Human Rights, and Structural Equality)
detail: Elimination of structural and cultural violence. • Ref: Pages 129-130

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
________ and ________ observed that Peace education cultivates the knowledge base, skills, attitudes and values that seek to transform people's mindsets, attitudes and behaviours.
back: Loreta Castro and Jasmin Galace (2010)
detail: Transformative peace education paradigm. • Ref: Pages 130-131

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
According to UNESCO (2024), the transformative goals of peace education have the following dimensions: ________.
back: Cognitive (knowledge/critical thinking), Socio-emotional (empathy/tolerance/dialogue), and Behavioural (action for social justice/peacebuilding)
detail: Head, heart, and hand framework of peace education. • Ref: Pages 131-132

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q10]
Briefly elaborate on the transformative goals mentioned above: (i) Cognitive, (ii) Socio-emotional, (iii) Behavioural.
back: (i) Cognitive: Understanding the roots of conflict, historical injustices, and human rights. (ii) Socio-emotional: Developing deep empathy, emotional self-regulation, compassion, and appreciation of cultural diversity. (iii) Behavioural: Engaging in active non-violent resistance, community dialogue, restorative mediation, and collaborative civic action.
detail: Holistic human development for peaceful coexistence. • Ref: Pages 131-133

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q11]
What is Intrapersonal peace education?
back: Education that fosters inner peace, emotional self-awareness, mindfulness, psychological balance, and self-acceptance within the individual mind.
detail: Inner harmony prerequisite to peaceful external interactions. • Ref: Pages 133-134

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q12]
What is the relevance of moral education?
back: It instills ethical values, moral reasoning, social conscience, integrity, and respect for the dignity of every human being, thereby discouraging predatory behaviour and corruption.
detail: Moral compass essential for civic responsibility. • Ref: Pages 134-135

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q13]
What is Interpersonal peace education and what is its scope?
back: Education focused on constructive communication, conflict handling skills, empathy, active listening, and cooperation in one-on-one and family relationships.
detail: Scope covers resolving peer bullying, marital discord, and neighborly disputes without violence. • Ref: Pages 135-136

chapter_title: Peace Education and Peace Practice
front:
[Workbook Review Q14]
What are peacebuilding activities in peace education?
back: Practical experiential initiatives such as peer mediation clubs, inter-ethnic youth camps, community service, peace drama/arts festivals, and grassroots reconciliation workshops.
detail: Translating classroom theory into real community impact. • Ref: Pages 136-138

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q1]
One of the most significant frameworks for analyzing conflict handling styles was proposed by ________ in 1974.
back: Kenneth W. Thomas and Ralph H. Kilmann (Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument - TKI)
detail: Maps handling styles along two dimensions: Assertiveness and Cooperativeness. • Ref: Page 142

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q2]
The ________ style is characterized by high assertiveness and low cooperativeness.
back: Competing (Dominating / Forcing)
detail: Focuses on winning at the other party's expense ('I win, you lose'). • Ref: Pages 142-143

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q3]
In assertive and uncooperative situations, the frequent results are ________ outcome.
back: Win-Lose (Zero-Sum)
detail: One party prevails through power, coercion, or positional rank. • Ref: Page 143

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q4]
In what situations is the competing style often appropriate?
back: In vital emergencies requiring swift, decisive action; when enforcing unpopular but crucial organizational rules; or when defending against predatory exploitation.
detail: Effective only when speed and decisiveness outweigh relationship building. • Ref: Pages 143-144

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q5]
What are the major disadvantages of the competing style?
back: It severely damages long-term relationships, provokes deep resentment and retaliation, stifles constructive input, and creates a hostile climate.
detail: High interpersonal costs and post-decision resistance. • Ref: Page 144

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q6]
In ________, individuals are committed to finding solutions that satisfy all parties' concerns. The general result of this scenario is ________ outcome.
back: Collaborating (Integrating / Problem-Solving); Win-Win (Synergistic)
detail: High assertiveness and high cooperativeness. • Ref: Pages 144-145

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q7]
The collaborating style is most applicable in situations such as ________.
back: When both parties' concerns are too vital to compromise; when combining diverse perspectives for innovative solutions; and when securing long-term stakeholder commitment.
detail: Best mode for complex, high-stakes organizational issues. • Ref: Pages 145-146

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
The major shortcomings of the collaborating style are that ________.
back: It demands immense time and energy, requires high trust and transparency, and can lead to analysis paralysis if overused on minor trivial issues.
detail: Resource-intensive conflict mode. • Ref: Page 146

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
The conflict handling style that is moderately assertive and moderately cooperative is ________.
back: Compromising (Sharing / Negotiating)
detail: Both parties give up something to find an acceptable middle ground. • Ref: Pages 146-147

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q10]
In compromising, mutual concessions mean ________.
back: Each party splits the difference and surrenders a portion of their goals in exchange for reciprocal concessions ('Give-and-take').
detail: Expedient resolution where neither party gets 100% of their desires. • Ref: Page 147

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q11]
Compromising style is usually suitable in ________.
back: When goals are moderately important but not worth disruption; when two opponents with equal power are firmly locked in stalemate; or as a temporary settlement under deadline pressure.
detail: Pragmatic intermediate solution. • Ref: Pages 147-148

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q12]
The major shortcoming of the compromising style is that ________.
back: It may yield sub-optimal, patched-over solutions that fail to address underlying root issues, potentially causing grievances to re-ignite later.
detail: Lose-Lose element where everyone leaves partly dissatisfied. • Ref: Page 148

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q13]
The conflict handling style that is characterized by low assertiveness and low cooperativeness is ________.
back: Avoiding (Withdrawing / Sidestepping)
detail: Diplomatic withdrawal or postponing action. • Ref: Pages 148-149

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q14]
In conflict handling style, avoidance means ________.
back: Deliberately ignoring, postponing, or withdrawing from a conflict rather than directly confronting the issues or other parties.
detail: 'I lose, you lose' mode of non-engagement. • Ref: Page 149

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q15]
Avoidance can be strategically effective where ________.
back: The issue is trivial; emotional tensions are too volatile and cooling-off time is needed; or when others can resolve the conflict more effectively.
detail: Tactical de-escalation pause. • Ref: Pages 149-150

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q16]
What are the major shortcomings of avoidance?
back: Important problems remain festering and unaddressed; decisions are made by default; and conflict parties experience mounting resentment and frustration.
detail: Chronic avoidance causes explosive future confrontations. • Ref: Page 150

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q17]
________ is a conflict-handling style in which one person puts the other party's needs, interests, or concerns ahead of their own in order to maintain harmony or preserve a relationship.
back: Accommodating (Obliging / Smoothing)
detail: Low assertiveness and high cooperativeness ('You win, I lose'). • Ref: Pages 150-151

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q18]
The major feature of accommodating is that it essentially prioritizes ________.
back: Preserving the relationship and communal peace over winning one's personal substantive agenda
detail: Relationship maintenance strategy. • Ref: Page 151

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q19]
What is self-sacrifice in accommodating and what is its major advantage?
back: Self-sacrifice means willingly conceding one's position to satisfy another; its major advantage is that it restores harmony, builds social capital, and demonstrates goodwill.
detail: Generates reciprocity and de-escalates explosive hostility. • Ref: Pages 151-152

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q20]
What conflict handling style happens when one or both parties refuse to compromise or let go of certain interests but decide to deal decisively with the other party?
back: Confrontation (Fighting / Coercive Contention)
detail: Escalation into adversarial battle of wills. • Ref: Pages 152-153

chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance
front:
[Workbook Review Q21]
What is emotional intelligence in conflict handling and explain: (i) Emotions as information, (ii) Emotional arousal and cognitive functioning.
back: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize, understand, manage, and constructively influence emotions during disputes. (i) Emotions as information: Emotions signal unmet needs and underlying values. (ii) Emotional arousal and cognitive functioning: Extreme anger or fear triggers amygdala hijack, reducing rational cognitive processing and escalating destructive reactions.
detail: Emotional self-regulation is critical for de-escalating confrontations. • Ref: Pages 155-158

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q1]
Peace Psychology evolved as an area of academic study in the second half of the ________.
back: Twentieth (20th) century (during the Cold War in the 1960s–1980s)
detail: Spurred by existential threats of nuclear confrontation and mass violence. • Ref: Page 161

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q2]
The incidence of peace, conflict, and violence brought together the key practices that define the field of ________.
back: Peace Psychology
detail: Intersection of psychological science and peace studies. • Ref: Page 161

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q3]
According to Galtung (1969), peace psychology aims to create theories and practices for the prevention and control of ________.
back: Violence (Direct, Structural, and Cultural violence)
detail: Holistic violence framework of peace research. • Ref: Pages 161-162

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q4]
________ builds on the concepts of mental processes and behaviour of war and peace.
back: Peace Psychology
detail: Applies cognitive, emotional, and social psychology to conflict transformation. • Ref: Page 162

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q5]
The tendency of individuals and groups to be involved in violent episodes or its prevention and mitigation is found in their patterns of ________.
back: Psychological socialization, cognitive schemas, and perceptions of threat/injustice
detail: Human behavior is mediated by internal cognitive and affective filters. • Ref: Pages 162-163

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q6]
According to Eze (2017), ________ is the maintenance of minimal conditions that enable efficient social processes in human society.
back: Peace (Social Order)
detail: Operational definition of societal stability. • Ref: Page 163

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q7]
A human action that wards off violence and facilitates nonviolent management of conflict is referred to as ________.
back: Peacemaking / Nonviolent Action
detail: Proactive constructive interventions stopping kinetic aggression. • Ref: Pages 163-164

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
Actions that promote the conditions that ensure social justice and minimize conflict are regarded as ________.
back: Peacebuilding
detail: Constructing durable structural conditions for long-term equity. • Ref: Page 164

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
According to Christie et al. (2001), peace psychology seeks to develop theories and practices aimed at ________ and mitigating ________ and ________ violence.
back: preventing; direct (episodic); structural
detail: Standard definition adopted by APA Division 48 (Society for the Study of Peace, Conflict, and Violence). • Ref: Pages 164-165

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q10]
Interpersonal or social conflict is defined as the perception of ________, while ________ refers to coercive actions carried out with the intention of harming others.
back: incompatible goals or scarce resources; violence
detail: Distinction between conflict (cognitive incompatibility) and violence (harmful behavioral act). • Ref: Pages 165-166

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q11]
What is Episodic violence?
back: Discrete, acute, and manifest acts of physical harm, assault, armed combat, or riots occurring at a specific time and place.
detail: Direct, visible violence with easily identifiable perpetrators and victims. • Ref: Page 166

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q12]
What is structural violence?
back: Systemic and institutional mechanisms (poverty, discriminatory laws, caste systems, apartheid) that prevent individuals and groups from meeting their basic needs and realizing their full human potential.
detail: Coined by Johan Galtung: violence built into social structures without an explicit individual assailant. • Ref: Pages 166-167

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q13]
According to the Society for the Study of Peace, Conflict, and Violence (2006), the goals of Peace Psychology are ________.
back: To understand psychological causes of conflict, apply psychological knowledge to reduce violence, and promote social justice and sustainable peace
detail: Official mandate of APA Division 48. • Ref: Pages 167-168

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q14]
The vision of peace psychologists is ________.
back: A world where human disputes are addressed through non-violent dialogue, empathy, reconciliation, and structural justice
detail: Transforming adversarial dynamics into collaborative co-existence. • Ref: Page 168

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q15]
Briefly outline the aims of Peace Psychology: (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi).
back: (i) Analyzing psychological roots of hatred, dehumanization, and intergroup bias. (ii) Mitigating trauma and PTSD in post-war populations. (iii) Fostering intergroup contact and empathy across historical divides. (iv) Promoting non-violent conflict resolution skills in schools and communities. (v) Challenging structural and cultural violence. (vi) Supporting truth, healing, and reconciliation processes.
detail: Comprehensive clinical and social peace psychology agenda. • Ref: Pages 168-170

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q16]
Who proposed the concepts of positive peace and negative peace?
back: Johan Galtung (1964, 1969)
detail: Foundational dichotomy of international peace research. • Ref: Page 170

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q17]
What is positive peace?
back: The presence of social justice, equality, institutional fairness, human rights, and the total absence of both direct and structural violence.
detail: Sustainable flourishing of society. • Ref: Pages 170-171

chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation
front:
[Workbook Review Q18]
What is negative peace?
back: The mere absence of direct, active physical violence or war, even while underlying injustices, oppression, and fear persist.
detail: Unstable ceasefires without systemic justice. • Ref: Pages 171-172

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q1]
The major legal instrument for the defence of human rights in Nigeria derives from the ________.
back: 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Chapter IV: Fundamental Rights)
detail: Sections 33 to 44 guarantee fundamental human rights (Right to life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, etc.). • Ref: Page 179

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q2]
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights to which Nigeria is a signatory is an example of a ________.
back: Multilateral International Human Rights Treaty / Global Normative Instrument
detail: Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948. • Ref: Pages 179-180

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q3]
________ establishes the legal framework and other mechanisms to hold government accountable in the event they violate human rights.
back: Constitutionalism (The Rule of Law and Judicial Review)
detail: Limits arbitrary government power through independent courts. • Ref: Page 180

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q4]
Legal framework can be viewed from ________ and ________ dimensions.
back: Substantive (statutory laws, rights, doctrines) and Procedural / Institutional (courts, enforcement agencies, rules of litigation)
detail: Two interdependent pillars of any jurisprudence system. • Ref: Pages 180-181

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q5]
________ provides a basis for enforcing law and policies that promote order, justice and fairness.
back: The Legal Framework / The Constitution
detail: Supreme law of the land from which all institutional legitimacy derives (Section 1(1) & 1(3)). • Ref: Page 181

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q6]
Legal framework can best be conceptualized as ________.
back: A coherent system of interrelated laws, judicial precedents, constitutional principles, and regulatory institutions that govern societal behavior and arbitrate disputes
detail: The bedrock of modern democratic governance. • Ref: Pages 181-182

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q7]
According to FasterCapital (2024), a legal framework provides ________.
back: Legal predictability, contractual certainty, protection of property rights, and institutional checks and balances
detail: Essential for conflict resolution and socio-economic investment. • Ref: Page 182

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
The growth of Nigeria's legal system has been linked to ________.
back: English Common Law tradition, Islamic (Sharia) Law, and Indigenous Customary Law (the tripartite legal heritage)
detail: Pluralistic nature of Nigerian jurisprudence. • Ref: Pages 182-184

chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
Human rights issues have been a subject for debate in ________ and ________ circles since the ________ and ________ until the present democratic government.
back: academic and civil society / political; colonial era and military regimes
detail: Long struggles against authoritarian decrees to achieve constitutional democracy. • Ref: Pages 184-186

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q1]
Community policing differs significantly from conventional policing approaches that stress coercive authority, ________, and ________.
back: Reactive incident response, state-centric hierarchy, and bureaucratic isolation
detail: Shift from authoritarian policing to democratic, service-oriented problem-solving. • Ref: Pages 199-200

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q2]
________ encourages cooperation between law enforcement officers and the communities they serve.
back: Community Policing
detail: Pioneered by Sir Robert Peel: 'The police are the public and the public are the police.' • Ref: Page 200

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q3]
The notion of community policing holds that security is a shared duty of the state, residents, community leaders, civil society groups, and ________.
back: Traditional institutions / Local vigilante formations / Private business sector
detail: Multi-stakeholder security governance model. • Ref: Pages 200-201

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q4]
Community policing seeks to identify and address the root causes of crime and social unrest via ________.
back: Proactive problem-solving, intelligence-led collaboration, and grassroots dialogue
detail: Addressing underlying socio-economic drivers rather than only reacting after crimes occur. • Ref: Pages 201-202

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q5]
Nigeria's diverse ________ and ________ backgrounds can lead to ________ tensions and localized conflicts that traditional enforcement techniques struggle to address effectively.
back: ethnic and religious; sectarian / communal
detail: Cultural diversity requires culturally nuanced dispute resolution. • Ref: Pages 202-203

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q6]
Traditional enforcement is particularly problematic in ________ and ________ where distrust in government institutions endures.
back: Rural agrarian communities and informal urban slums / marginalized settlements
detail: Deep historical suspicion of armed police tactical units. • Ref: Page 203

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q7]
Community policing is increasingly recognised as a strategic technique for connecting institutions with the ________ they serve.
back: Grassroots citizens (local communities)
detail: Bridges the legitimacy gap between law enforcement and citizens. • Ref: Pages 203-204

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
Kenku and Umar (2025) argue that ________.
back: Community policing provides the vital architecture for rebuilding public confidence in Nigeria's internal security apparatus
detail: Recent academic verification of policing reforms. • Ref: Pages 204-205

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
According to Aremu et al. (2024), constant involvement between police officers and community people improved ________, ________, and ________, and aided in the resolution of communal conflicts in urban environments.
back: Mutual trust, actionable intelligence sharing, and timely dispute mediation
detail: Empirical study on urban community policing in Nigeria. • Ref: Pages 205-206

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q10]
According to Aremu et al. (2024), community policing can improve security governance by encouraging ________ and ________ for maintaining peace and order.
back: Shared ownership and civic co-responsibility
detail: Citizens shift from passive observers to active security partners. • Ref: Page 206

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q11]
Community policing projects help to create ________.
back: Safe spaces and structured community-police consultative forums
detail: Regular platforms for joint safety planning. • Ref: Pages 206-207

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q12]
Community policing creates platforms for conversation and collaboration, allowing ________, ________, and ________ to actively participate in identifying potential conflict.
back: Youth leaders, women groups, and traditional elders / religious figures
detail: Inclusive community representation. • Ref: Page 207

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q13]
In restive environments, collaborative community policing initiatives can serve as ________ and prevent disagreements from escalating into ________.
back: Early warning and de-escalation buffers; violent communal warfare / bloodshed
detail: Preventing skirmishes from turning into full-scale communal clashes. • Ref: Pages 207-208

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q14]
In Kogi State, cooperative community-based security measures including ________, ________, and ________ have improved public safety and strengthened local responses to criminal activity.
back: Joint community vigilante patrols, hunter associations integration, and local intelligence taskforces
detail: Case study of hybrid sub-national security collaboration. • Ref: Pages 208-209

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q15]
In Anambra State, community policing measures were found to have ________ in ________ and resulted in improved local safety.
back: curbed armed robbery and kidnapping; commercial trading hubs and transit towns
detail: Anambra Vigilante Group (AVG) and neighborhood watch partnership. • Ref: Pages 209-210

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q16]
Community policing in Nigeria faces two types of challenges namely ________ and ________.
back: Internal/Structural challenges and External/Societal challenges
detail: Systemic institutional and socio-political impediments. • Ref: Pages 210-211

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q17]
Some of the major challenges of community policing in Nigeria are ________.
back: Inadequate funding and modern logistics, deep historical public distrust from police brutality, political interference by state governors, and poor welfare of personnel
detail: Cripples implementation fidelity across state commands. • Ref: Pages 211-212

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q18]
What is a community?
back: A social unit or group of people living within a shared geographical area or bound by common interests, traditions, cultural identity, and mutual interdependence.
detail: Sociological definition combining geography, shared values, and mutual ties. • Ref: Page 212

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q19]
Communities are more than just physical locations; they are complex social systems marked by ________.
back: Interconnected kinship networks, shared values, historical memories, and social norms
detail: Relational understanding of community. • Ref: Pages 212-213

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q20]
Communities are critical forums for ________ and ________, where collective norms impact conduct and disagreements are typically addressed using culturally established procedures such as ________ and ________.
back: Socialization and collective identity; elder conciliation and traditional customary arbitration
detail: Endogenous African conflict resolution mechanisms. • Ref: Pages 213-214

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q21]
What is policing?
back: The organized social function of maintaining public order, enforcing laws, preventing and detecting crime, and protecting lives and property in a society.
detail: Distinction between the police as an institution and policing as a broad societal function. • Ref: Page 214

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q22]
The primary responsibilities of the police include the following: ________, ________, and ________.
back: Protection of life and property, preservation of public law and order, and apprehension and prosecution of offenders
detail: Statutory duties under Section 4 of the Nigeria Police Act. • Ref: Pages 214-215

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q23]
Contemporary policing and maintaining order necessitates the involvement of a wide range of stakeholders, including ________.
back: Community elders, youth councils, vigilante networks, civil society organizations, and private security companies
detail: Pluralization of contemporary security architecture. • Ref: Page 215

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q24]
Adeyemi and Bamidele (2024) posit that contemporary policing ________.
back: Must transition from an antagonistic military-era force into a transparent, rights-respecting civilian service accountable to the people
detail: Democratization of policing imperatives. • Ref: Pages 215-216

chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution
front:
[Workbook Review Q25]
What is community policing?
back: A philosophy and organizational strategy that promotes proactive partnership between law enforcement and citizens to solve crime, fear of crime, and neighborhood social disorders.
detail: Standard criminological definition. • Ref: Page 216

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q1]
________ were originally created as crucial frameworks for conflict prevention.
back: Conflict Early Warning Systems (CEWS)
detail: Designed to detect tensions before violence erupts. • Ref: Page 217

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q2]
________ is a structured approach that entails gathering and examining data to recognize possible threats prior to their emergence.
back: Early Warning
detail: Information-driven preventive mechanism. • Ref: Pages 217-218

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q3]
________ defines early warning as a tool that alerts decision makers to the potential outbreak, escalation and resurgence of violent conflict.
back: The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) / United Nations
detail: International diplomatic definition. • Ref: Page 218

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q4]
________ involves actions taken immediately after a threat is recognized, focused on managing, resolving, or preventing violence or disaster.
back: Early Response
detail: Connecting warning data to proactive interventions. • Ref: Pages 218-219

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q5]
Early response measures might include ________.
back: Preventive diplomacy, mediation deployment, police peace patrols, public dialogue, and humanitarian pre-positioning
detail: Diverse political, judicial, and tactical response actions. • Ref: Pages 219-220

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q6]
What is risk knowledge?
back: The comprehensive understanding of hazards, vulnerabilities, and community exposure to conflict or disaster dynamics within a given territory.
detail: Baseline empirical foundation for warning systems. • Ref: Page 220

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q7]
What are the components of risk knowledge?
back: Hazard identification, vulnerability assessment, capacity analysis, and exposure mapping
detail: The 4 core elements of risk assessment. • Ref: Pages 220-221

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q8]
________ entails systematic observation to detect early signs of emerging threats and the generation of warnings when predefined thresholds are approached or exceeded.
back: Monitoring and Warning Service (Threat Surveillance)
detail: Second pillar of early warning systems. • Ref: Pages 221-222

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q9]
________ ensures that warnings reach decision-makers, response actors, and at-risk populations in time for action to be taken.
back: Dissemination and Communication
detail: Effective channels including SMS alerts, radios, and secure policy briefs. • Ref: Pages 222-223

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q10]
________ encompasses preparedness measures, contingency plans, resources, and institutional arrangements enabling timely and effective action once a warning is received.
back: Response Capability
detail: Closing the critical 'Warning-Response Gap'. • Ref: Pages 223-224

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q11]
What are the challenges to response capability?
back: Lack of political will by leaders, bureaucratic bottlenecks, poor funding, logistical deficits, and skepticism regarding intelligence accuracy
detail: Why warnings often fail to prevent atrocities. • Ref: Pages 224-225

chapter_title: Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Systems
front:
[Workbook Review Q12]
Briefly explain the following Operational Levels of early warning systems: (i) Top-down systems, (ii) Bottom-up systems, (iii) Hybrid approaches; and the following Methodologies: (iv) Indicator-based, (v) Predictive machine learning, (vi) Event-based surveillance.
back: (i) Top-down: State-centric, intelligence-driven, and managed by national security agencies. (ii) Bottom-up: Grassroots, community-based monitoring by citizens and local NGOs. (iii) Hybrid: Blends satellite/state data with grassroots reporting (e.g. WANEP/ECOWARN). (iv) Indicator-based: Tracks structured qualitative/quantitative indices (hate speech index, arms prices). (v) Predictive ML: Uses big data and machine learning to forecast conflict probability. (vi) Event-based: Monitors sudden trigger incidents in real time.
detail: Comprehensive typology of modern early warning architectures. • Ref: Pages 225-230
